findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Highways, Transport, Planning and Development
findings.paper_title: Highways Capital Programme from 2026-2027 and year end outturn of the 2025-2026 Programme
findings.headline: Environment Agency flood defence grant funding reduced; 2026/27 bids exceeded budget by wider margin than historical trend
findings.detail: The six-year EA investment programme ended early in 2025/26, pausing flood defence funding. For 2026/27, bids for flood defence funding exceeded available budget by a greater margin than previously experienced, indicating growing unmet flood management needs.
findings.matters: Declining external flood defence funding means the council cannot deliver all identified flood risk management schemes, deferring asset protection during an era of increased climate risk.
findings.figures: EA funding pause in 2025/26; 2026/27 bid oversubscription described as exceeding the historical margin
findings.quote: Bids for funding during the first year of this period (2026/27) exceeded the available budget by a greater margin than previously seen.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Highways, Transport, Planning and Development
findings.paper_title: Highways Capital Programme from 2026-2027 and year end outturn of the 2025-2026 Programme
findings.headline: 2025/26 Maintenance Block overspent; additional funding drawn from other sources to cover variance
findings.detail: The highways maintenance budget exceeded its allocation during 2025/26 due to unprogrammed reactive maintenance schemes, requiring the council to reallocate funds from other areas to cover the shortfall.
findings.matters: Material maintenance budget overruns indicate either deteriorating asset condition driving reactive work, or poor budget forecasting; either suggests future budget pressures.
findings.figures: 2025/26 Maintenance Block overspend; amount unspecified but significant enough to require reallocation
findings.quote: The impact of unprogrammed reactive schemes is that the 2025/26 Maintenance Block budget was overspent and required additional funding from other sources.

findings.committee: Executive Cabinet Member Highways, Transport, Planning and Development
findings.paper_title: Highways Capital Programme from 2026-2027 and year end outturn of the 2025-2026 Programme
findings.headline: Bridge and structures asset management budgets acknowledged as inadequate for anything beyond emergency repairs
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it cannot fund preventative maintenance on highway structures and bridges, only reactive maintenance and emergency works. This forces a reactive posture on critical infrastructure with deferred asset renewal.
findings.matters: Chronic underfunding of preventative bridge maintenance creates a deteriorating asset base and eventual need for emergency capital spending or service disruption.
findings.figures: Bridge maintenance budget of £1053k against a forward programme covering 8+ years of works, with inadequacy acknowledged
findings.quote: Despite utilising an electronic bridge management system, asset management for highway structures and the forward planning of workloads continues to be extremely challenging because budgets are inadequate to cover anything beyond reactive maintenance and emergency works.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee Risk Update June 2026 Appendix
findings.headline: Escalating children's services placement costs with no funded solution, may force use of unregulated providers
findings.detail: Corporate Risk CR6 flags increasing costs of placements for children with complex needs transitioning to adulthood, limited availability of suitable options. Risk rated High (4x3=12). The council faces inability to provide appropriate placements and risk of forced use of unregulated providers with potential legal and reputational damage.
findings.matters: This is unfunded demand inflation in a statutory service; it signals a structural gap between needs and resources that must show up as either service rationing or deficit.
findings.figures: Risk rating 4x3=12 (High); 6-month target 4x3=12 (High)
findings.quote: Increasing costs of placements for children transitioning into adulthood, driven by higher needs including the complex care needs of some service users and limited availability of suitable options, could result the Council being unable to provide appropriate placements, sustain current arrangements or have no choice but to use unregulated providers.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee Risk Update June 2026 Appendix
findings.headline: Workforce turnover and recruitment costs rising in competitive labour market with ageing workforce
findings.detail: Corporate Risk CR4 flags turnover and recruitment challenges in a competitive job market and ageing workforce driving increased operational costs (agency and recruitment) and service delivery risk. Rated High (4x3=12) with no expected improvement.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled agency and recruitment cost inflation is a live driver of budget overrun; the council's stated appetite to operate 'below target capacity' signals it expects permanent structural underfunding.
findings.figures: Risk rating 4x3=12 (High); 6-month target 4x3=12 (High)
findings.quote: Due to turnover and recruitment challenges in a competitive job market and ageing workforce there is a risk of further reduced capability and capacity leading to increased operational costs (agency & recruitment costs) and risk to service delivery.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee Risk Update June 2026 Appendix
findings.headline: Council unable to maintain balanced budget in 2026/27 and fulfil statutory services
findings.detail: Corporate Risk CR2 rates financial instability as High (4x3=12) with no expected improvement (6-month target 4x3=12). The council is formally documenting that there is material risk of budget deficit and inability to deliver statutory services in the next financial year. Budget monitoring 2026/27 is flagged as a new action.
findings.matters: This is an explicit statement in the formal risk register that the council faces material risk of deficit and service failure in the coming year—the core scenario that affects lending decisions.
findings.figures: Risk rating 4x3=12 (High); 6-month target 4x3=12 (High); no reduction expected
findings.quote: Financial instability means the Council is unable to maintain a balanced budget in 2026/27 and fulfil statutory services.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Internal Audit Annual Opinion and Report
findings.headline: Council has not yet demonstrated compliance with CIPFA Financial Management Code
findings.detail: A desktop review of compliance with the CIPFA Financial Management Code completed early in 2025/26 indicated that further work was required to demonstrate compliance and that the self-assessment needed to be updated. This will be an area of follow-up in 2026/27.
findings.matters: The CIPFA Code sets standards for financial management in councils; non-compliance indicates gaps in financial governance and internal controls that could impact financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Not yet compliant; self-assessment needs updating
findings.quote: A desktop review of compliance with the CIPFA Financial Management Code was completed early in the year, which indicated that further work was required to demonstrate compliance and the self-assessment needed to be updated.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Internal Audit Annual Opinion and Report
findings.headline: Albert Halls venue audit shows limited assurance with prior recommendations not implemented
findings.detail: A follow-up audit of Albert Halls, which had previously received limited assurance, found that recommendations relating to procurement of a drinks supplier and review of fees had not been implemented. Additionally, cash income procedures issues were identified. These matters were escalated to senior management and Chief Officers.
findings.matters: Limited assurance ratings indicate significant control weaknesses; failure to implement prior recommendations suggests management is not addressing known risks, and cash handling issues are a direct control failure.
findings.figures: Prior recommendations not implemented; cash income procedures issues identified
findings.quote: We found that recommendations relating to procurement of a drinks supplier and review of fees and changes had not been implemented. In addition, issues were found with cash income procedures.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Internal Audit Annual Opinion and Report
findings.headline: Building Control Services had systemic failures requiring substantial remediation
findings.detail: Internal concerns about Building Control systems and processes led to a voluntary Local Authority Building Control audit and inspection by the Building Safety Regulator. These reviews highlighted a wide range of areas for improvement across policy, processes, systems, and staffing. Substantial work has been completed to address these issues, though review work is still ongoing to assess past records for compliance.
findings.matters: Building Control is a statutory function with public safety implications; systemic failures of this scale indicate control and governance failures that required external intervention.
findings.figures: Wide range of areas for improvement identified; substantial remediation work required and ongoing
findings.quote: These reviews and work of Internal Audit highlighted a wide range of areas for improvement and substantial work has since been completed to address policy, processes, system and staffing issues. There is still some review work ongoing in assessing past records to assure compliance and this is ongoing.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Internal Audit Annual Opinion and Report
findings.headline: Internal audit function operating below required capacity with staffing vacancies
findings.detail: Completion of audit work in 2025/26 was impacted by vacancies in the Internal Audit team. The council acknowledges that capacity remains below required levels, and a strategy to address this will not be presented until 2026 as part of the Quality Assurance and Improvement Programme review.
findings.matters: Insufficient internal audit capacity undermines the council's assurance framework and its ability to identify control weaknesses across the organisation.
findings.figures: Staffing vacancies in Internal Audit; capacity below required levels
findings.quote: Completion of audit work in 2025/26 has been impacted by vacancies in the Internal Audit team. Capacity remains below required levels and a strategy to address this will be presented to CLT and to Audit Committee as part of the review of the Quality Assurance and Improvement Programme (QAIP) in 2026.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Internal Audit Annual Opinion and Report
findings.headline: Information security controls remain weak after year of remediation effort
findings.detail: The internal audit follow-up on information security breaches in 2025/26 again concluded with limited assurance, the same rating as 2024/25. Of 10 moderate to significant recommendations made in the prior year, only one was fully implemented and four were partially implemented. A revised action plan has been proposed.
findings.matters: Persistent control weaknesses in data and system security over a two-year period indicate the council is not effectively addressing known vulnerabilities, which is a material control risk.
findings.figures: 1 of 10 recommendations fully implemented; 4 of 10 partially implemented
findings.quote: The follow-up audit again found limited assurance, with only one recommendation fully implemented and four partially implemented out of 10 moderate to significant recommendations made.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Audit assessment found gaps in visibility and consistency of procurement governance across the council.
findings.detail: An audit assessment of Procurement Act compliance and management review identified that whilst some areas show strong practice, there is a need for assurance over consistency of approach across all procurement activities. An improvement plan will be delivered in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Procurement governance gaps affect value for money, contract management, and financial controls over a significant spend area.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Whilst there are areas of strong commissioning and procurement practice within the Council there is a need for assurance over the consistency of approach across all activities.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Audit review has identified opportunities to strengthen information governance oversight across the council.
findings.detail: Internal audit and management reviews have confirmed gaps in the oversight of information governance arrangements. A Business Improvement Review is underway to assess approach and structures, with reporting expected by December 2026.
findings.matters: Weak information governance oversight poses risks to data security, regulatory compliance, and operational resilience.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Internal Audit and management reviews have confirmed opportunities to strengthen the oversight of information governance arrangements across the Council to both strengthen corporate functions and ensure engagement of directorates and departments in information governance standards and compliance

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Risk management framework is inconsistent and has not been updated regularly.
findings.detail: The council identifies that risk management strategy and framework for review of risks at strategic and directorate level lacks consistency. A new Risk Management Strategy has been agreed, but effectiveness over a full year cycle is still required, and this will remain a reported governance challenge until embedded.
findings.matters: Inconsistent risk management frameworks may result in gaps in visibility of emerging financial and operational risks.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Risk management strategy and framework for review of risks at strategic and directorate level is inconsistent and has not been updated on a regular basis.

findings.paper_title: 24.6.26 Audit Committee 25_26 Draft Annual Governance Statement
findings.headline: Internal Audit resources have been reduced significantly, limiting delivery of the annual audit plan.
findings.detail: The statement acknowledges that reduced internal audit capacity has constrained the council's ability to deliver a full audit plan. A resourcing strategy is being developed to address this, with outline plans to be shared with Audit Committee and stakeholders by end September 2026.
findings.matters: Reduced internal audit capacity directly weakens the control environment and reduces oversight of financial systems, compliance and controls — a material risk for lenders assessing financial control robustness.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Internal Audit resources are reduced significantly and this has limited the ability to deliver the annual audit plan as reported to Audit Committee.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Building Control investigation underway following allegations of significant failings
findings.detail: The auditor reports: 'Internal Audit are carrying out an investigation within Building Control. This is following allegations regarding a number of significant failings within the department. The Council have reacted appropriately to the allegations made and have included reference to the issue within their revised 2024/25 Financial Statements.' While the Council has reacted appropriately, this signals control breakdowns in a revenue-generating service.
findings.matters: Service failures in Building Control, especially those serious enough to trigger investigation, indicate governance gaps and carry reputational and financial risk.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Internal Audit are carrying out an investigation within Building Control. This is following allegations regarding a number of significant failings within the department.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Internal Audit resource constraints forcing reprioritisation of audit plan and reducing assurance coverage
findings.detail: The auditor notes that Internal Audit's 2024/25 Annual Opinion was 'reasonable assurance,' but this was delivered against constrained resources. 'Internal Audit have had to reprioritise the audit plan to focus delivery on higher risk areas.' The auditor further states: 'Going forwards, the Audit Committee will need to continue to monitor closely the delivery of the internal audit programme to ensure that the necessary assurance is being provided.' This indicates the Council's ability to identify control breakdowns and risks is compromised.
findings.matters: Underfunded internal audit means the Council's internal control environment is monitored less thoroughly, reducing early warning of problems.
findings.figures: None specific
findings.quote: Internal Audit have had to reprioritise the audit plan to focus delivery on higher risk areas. Going forwards, the Audit Committee will need to continue to monitor closely the delivery of the internal audit programme to ensure that the necessary assurance is being provided.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Auditor identifies continuing governance weakness: Corporate Risk Register still inadequately embedded despite prior-year recommendation
findings.detail: The auditor identified a continuing significant weakness in governance arrangements. Although the Council took steps in 2024/25 to address this—refreshing the Risk Management Strategy and reporting the Corporate Risk Register to the Audit Committee in December 2024—the auditor found the weakness 'has not been fully addressed and still exists for 2024/25.' The issue is that 'the infrequency of the Corporate Risk Registers review and reporting is evidence the significant weakness in arrangements still exists.' This was flagged as a weakness in the prior year but not properly resolved.
findings.matters: Weak corporate risk management and governance means the Council may not be identifying and monitoring strategic risks effectively, leaving it vulnerable to emerging pressures.
findings.figures: None specific, but weakness flagged as continuing from prior year
findings.quote: Whilst the Council has made positive steps to address this weakness in 2024/25, the infrequency of the Corporate Risk Registers review and reporting is evidence the significant weakness in arrangements still exists.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: 2025/26 forecast overspend of £22m (at Q2), significantly larger than 2024/25, with savings delivery lagging
findings.detail: The auditor reviewed the Q2 2025/26 financial report, which forecasts a £22m overspend for the year, largely driven by Children's Services pressures. The Council identified £3.159m of savings, but only £2.664m had been delivered as at Q2. Importantly, the auditor notes the forecasted overspend 'will need to be met through the use of corporate reserves.' This indicates the Council's 2025/26 budget (approved at £604m with £7.8m identified savings and a further £3.7m of cuts required) is already in trouble only halfway through the year.
findings.matters: Deteriorating forecast overspends (£13.3m in 2024/25 rising to £22m forecast in 2025/26) show the Council is moving in the wrong direction financially, reinforcing that structural deficits are growing rather than being managed.
findings.figures: 2025/26 Q2 forecast overspend: £22m; Children's Services element: £20.8m; savings delivered £2.664m of £3.159m identified
findings.quote: We have reviewed the quarter two financial report for 2025/26 which is currently forecasting a £22m overspend for the year, this is largely because of significant pressures in Children's Services of £20.8m.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Children's Services demand pressures driving persistent overspends with no sustainable recovery plan visible
findings.detail: Children's Services delivered a £12.9m adverse variance in 2024/25 (out of £13.3m total Council overspend). The auditor attributes this to 'ongoing demand pressures on placements and the complexity of cases received.' For 2025/26, at Q2 reporting, Children's Services is forecasting a £20.8m overspend, 'primarily driven by SEN transport and the unplanned use of agency staff.' The auditor notes: 'Work is ongoing to recruit staff on a permanent basis. A recovery plan is in place to address the overspend in Children's Services but the quarter two report is clear that overspend will need to be met through the use of corporate reserves.'
findings.matters: A service with year-on-year structural deficits funded by reserves rather than solutions indicates demand is outrunning the Council's service model. This directly threatens financial sustainability as reserves are finite.
findings.figures: 2024/25: £12.9m overspend; 2025/26 Q2 forecast: £20.8m overspend
findings.quote: The in year overspend is driven primarily through the Children's Services directorate which had an adverse variance of £12.9m. The additional pressures seen in Children's Services is directly linked to ongoing demand pressures on placements and the complexity of cases received.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit spiralling to £35.5m by 2027/28, when statutory override protection ends
findings.detail: The DSG cumulative deficit increased from £13.7m to £15.1m in 2024/25 and is forecast to reach £22.5m at end of 2025/26 and £35.5m at end of 2027/28. The overspend is driven by the High Needs Block (Special Education Needs). Currently, a statutory override allows deficits to be charged to a separate reserve, protecting the general fund. However, this override ends in 2027/28. The Council is in receipt of Safety Valve Funding but this has not prevented the deficit from growing. The auditor states the Council has usable reserves that could fund the deficit, 'However, doing so would significantly impact the financial sustainability of the Council.'
findings.matters: When the statutory override expires, a £35.5m DSG deficit would have to be funded from the general fund, requiring either unsustainable reserve depletion or service cuts. The current trajectory shows the underlying drivers (complexity of cases, cost of provision) are not being managed.
findings.figures: DSG deficit 2024/25: £15.1m; forecast 2025/26: £22.5m; forecast 2027/28: £35.5m (when override ends)
findings.quote: The Council's Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) cumulative deficit is forecast increase to be £22.5m at the end of 2025/26 and reach £35.5m at the end of 2027/28, when the statutory override is due to end.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Usable reserves forecasted to be drawn down by £36m over three years, leaving only £15.1m by 2027/28
findings.detail: The Council's usable reserves decreased from £262.8m to £250.3m in 2024/25. The auditor notes the Council is forecasting to drawdown £36m of budget cashflow reserves between 2025/26 and 2027/28, which would leave a residual balance of only £15.1m. The Financial Resilience Reserve specifically fell from £20m to £13.5m in year. This planned depletion is a consequence of ongoing structural deficits and demonstrates unsustainable reliance on reserves to bridge funding gaps.
findings.matters: Reserves are a finite buffer against financial shocks. Forecasting to burn £36m over three years to cover operational deficits signals the Council is funding recurrent spending from non-recurrent sources, a key credit concern.
findings.figures: Usable reserves £250.3m (down from £262.8m); Financial Resilience Reserve £13.5m (down from £20m); forecasted drawdown £36m over 2025/26-2027/28, leaving £15.1m
findings.quote: The Council are forecasting to drawdown £36m of their budget cashflow reserves between 2025/26 and 2027/28, this would leave a residual balance of £15.1m remaining for use in future years.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Auditor's Annual Report
findings.headline: Auditor reports Council does not have adequate financial sustainability arrangements; significant weakness continues unaddressed from prior year
findings.detail: The auditor found a continuing significant weakness in financial sustainability because the Council has not addressed the underlying structural deficit. The Council set a balanced budget but delivered a £13.3m overspend in 2024/25, primarily through Children's Services (£12.9m adverse variance). The overspend was partially offset by a £18.5m favourable variance in Financial Services, which the auditor characterises as unsustainable and unplanned. No MTFS was reported to members in 2024/25, despite this being flagged as a weakness in the prior year. The auditor states: 'The failure to address the underlying deficit is evidence of a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements for financial sustainability.'
findings.matters: A lender assessing credit risk needs to know whether the council can deliver services within available resources without drawing down reserves. Continued structural deficits funded by one-off gains and reserves indicate deteriorating financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £13.3m outturn overspend 2024/25; £12.9m Children's Services variance; £18.5m Financial Services favourable variance; £22m forecasted overspend for 2025/26 (Q2 position)
findings.quote: The Council has faced a challenging financial year in 2024/25 with overspend of £13.3m. The favourable outturn position on Financial Services has allowed this to be partially offset however this is primarily through unsustainable and unplanned measures.

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Audit Completion Follow Up Letter
findings.headline: £22.02m in adjusted misstatements required during audit, including £7.7m lease liability corrections
findings.detail: The auditors had to correct £22.02m of errors across the group accounts, including £7.7m for right of use assets and lease liabilities omitted from draft statements, £6.31m pension adjustments, and multiple revaluation and classification errors. This large volume of audit corrections indicates control deficiencies.
findings.matters: Requiring corrections of this magnitude in lease assets and other major balance sheet items suggests material weaknesses in the accounting system, affecting the reliability of interim reporting and the council's control environment.
findings.figures: £22.02m total adjusted misstatements; £7.7m lease liabilities; £6.31m pension adjustments
findings.quote: There are five adjusted misstatements and two disclosure adjustments... Total adjusted misstatements 22,020

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Audit Completion Follow Up Letter
findings.headline: £3m overstatement of property gross value with £1.35m impact on reported financial performance
findings.detail: The council overstated the gross value movement of assets not revalued in year by £3m and failed to account for this correctly in the comprehensive income and expenditure statement, creating a total extrapolated impact of £1.35m on reported results.
findings.matters: Errors in both asset valuation and reported financial performance reduce the reliability of accounts for assessing the council's true position and outturn against budget.
findings.figures: £3m overstatement, £1.35m CIES impact
findings.quote: Our testing of assets not revalued in year noted that the Council has overstated the gross value of the movement by £3m. In addition to, the Council have done their assessment and charged the net increase in value of these assets to Revaluation Reserve without considering the impact on Comprehensive Income and Expenditure Statement (CIES). The total extrapolated impact on the CIES is £1.35m

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Audit Completion Follow Up Letter
findings.headline: £3.678m extrapolated revaluation error in land and building valuations not corrected
findings.detail: Audit testing found differences in the areas and indices used for asset revaluations, with an extrapolated error of £3.678m. The council did not adjust this.
findings.matters: Unadjusted valuation errors in fixed assets affect the reliability of balance sheet figures and the council's reported asset base, which affects borrowing capacity and collateral assessment.
findings.quote: Our testing of the valuation of assets noted differences in the areas as well as the indexes used. The extrapolated error in relation to the variances noted is £3.678m

findings.paper_title: 2024-2025 Audit Completion Follow Up Letter
findings.headline: £7.848m understatement of pension fund assets left unadjusted by the council
findings.detail: The Greater Manchester Pension Fund auditor identified an understatement of assets held by the fund. The council's share of this understatement is estimated at £7.848m on the pension asset. This material error was not corrected in the accounts.
findings.matters: An unadjusted pension liability of this magnitude is a hidden liability affecting balance sheet reliability and the council's actual financial position, which directly impacts credit risk assessment.
findings.quote: The Pension Fund auditor reported to us an understatement of the assets held by Greater Manchester Pension Fund. Our estimate of the impact of this on the Council's pension liability, based on its share of the Pension Fund assets, is £7.848m.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Current-year (2025-26) overspends of £22m will drain reserves to the point where they may fall below the auditor-recommended minimum
findings.detail: Q2 2025-26 directorate forecasts show a £22m overspend. The council expects to use approximately £20m of corporate reserves to balance the year-end position. The Borough Treasurer notes that this level of reserve use is 'not sustainable in the medium term.' With £17m of additional reserve depletion planned over the next four years, the reserve position is deteriorating rapidly.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves to cover recurring overspends is unsustainable and leaves the council with no buffer for shocks. If overspends continue or reserves fall below £14.16m (the advised minimum), the council enters a high-risk position.
findings.figures: £22m directorate overspend in Q2 2025-26; ~£20m reserve support expected; £17m total reserve depletion over MTFP
findings.quote: The use of this level of reserves to balance the annual financial out-turn position is not sustainable in the medium term.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: A £30m savings target is planned for 2027-28 to 2029-30, which the council itself describes as challenging to achieve
findings.detail: After 2026-27, Bolton faces an indicative cuts requirement of £30m over three years (roughly £10m per year). The Borough Treasurer's report explicitly states this will be 'challenging to achieve, and a significant programme of work will need to commence as soon as is practicable.' No detail of what these savings will be is provided.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether the council has a credible plan to deliver £30m of savings without service collapse or forced asset sales. The language suggests uncertainty about deliverability.
findings.figures: £30m savings target over 2027-28 to 2029-30; £10m per year indicative
findings.quote: It should be noted that the indicative cuts target for 2027/28 to 2029/30 is circa £30m. This will be challenging to achieve, and a significant programme of work will need to commence as soon as is practicable.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Children's Services is systemically underfunded and has required a budget uplift to match Greater Manchester peers
findings.detail: The council forecast a £20.8m overspend in Children's Services for Q2 2025-26. In response, it has determined that additional baseline budget allocation is needed for future years to bring funding into line with other Greater Manchester authorities. This signals structural underfunding of a demand-led service.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this uplift will stick, or whether demand will continue to exceed budget, forcing further reserve drawdowns or cuts elsewhere.
findings.figures: £20.8m overspend in Children's Services Q2 2025-26; demand pressure of £10m added for 2026-27
findings.quote: Following a review of the budgeted funding levels of Children's Services Directorate, it has been determined that additional budget allocation for future financial years is required to bring levels of funding to a position more broadly consistent with other authorities in local Greater Manchester.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Council is using reserves to balance the budget in a way external auditors have already flagged as unsustainable
findings.detail: Bolton is using £10.6m of reserves to balance the 2026-27 budget, with a total of £17m required over the 4-year MTFP. This approach was explicitly challenged by Forvis Mazars in their 2022-23 Value for Money report as unsustainable, yet the council continues down this path.
findings.matters: An auditor challenge to financial sustainability is a governance red flag. The council's own external auditors have already warned that this strategy is not sustainable, and the council is disregarding that warning.
findings.figures: £10.6m reserves for 2026-27; £17m reserves over 4-year MTFP
findings.quote: this approach to the use of reserves has previously been challenged by the Council's external auditors (Forvis Mazars LLP), in their 2022/23 Value for Money (VFM) report, as unsustainable.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27
findings.headline: DSG deficit will require council's own resources from 2028-29 onwards, after government support ends
findings.detail: Bolton held an £18m DSG deficit at the start of 2025-26, driven by High Needs Block overspends. Government has announced a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of deficits, but only until the Statutory Override ends on 31 March 2028. After that date, the council must fund any residual deficit from its own budget and reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can absorb a potentially large education deficit from its own resources within the next 2-3 years, or whether it signals structural insolvency risk.
findings.figures: £18m DSG deficit at start 2025-26; £8m High Needs Block in-year overspend forecast for 2025-26
findings.quote: Therefore, local authorities will need to plan to be able to meet the cost of the residual deficit from their own resources in 2028-29, including setting aside appropriate reserves in the preceding years.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 Appendix K - MTFP 26-27 to 29-30
findings.headline: Children's external residential placements increased 20% in one year with no quick fix acknowledged.
findings.detail: External residential placements for children increased 20% between October 2024 and September 2025, with annual weekly costs rising 7% over the same period. Individual placements cost £15k+ per week. The council explicitly acknowledges there is no quick fix to this problem, only ongoing work to manage demand.
findings.matters: This is material uncontrolled cost growth in a year already showing £20.8m Children's Services overspend, with no solution in sight and increasing likelihood of further budget pressure in an area that already consumes significant resources.
findings.figures: 20% placement increase (Oct 2024 to Sept 2025); 7% annual cost increase; £15k per week individual placement cost
findings.quote: The numbers of external residential placements for children had increased in September 2025 by 20% from October 2024, with an annual increase in weekly costs over the same period of 7%. It is acknowledged that there is no quick fix to this.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 Appendix K - MTFP 26-27 to 29-30
findings.headline: Current year 2025/26 is forecasting £22m overspend and the council explicitly states finding required cuts is becoming increasingly difficult.
findings.detail: At quarter two 2025/26, Bolton is already forecasting a £22m overspend. Children's Services alone shows £20.833m overspend driven by high-cost external placements. Going forward, the council requires £10m annual cuts in 2027/28–2029/30 but states it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify cuts that protect vulnerable people and minimise staff impact.
findings.matters: In-year overspends combined with acknowledged difficulty finding sustainable savings raise questions about whether the planned £10m annual cuts are achievable without service reductions, staff impacts, or further reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: £22m Q2 2025/26 overspend; £20.833m Children's Services; £10m annual cuts required years 3–4 of MTFP
findings.quote: The major risk at this present time is the Council's ability to deliver another cuts programme to balance the budget. It is clear that this is becoming increasingly difficult to identify cuts that meet the Council's policy of protecting the most vulnerable members of the community and minimising the impact on staff.

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 Appendix K - MTFP 26-27 to 29-30
findings.headline: Corporate budget reserves are being depleted using a strategy auditors have flagged as unsustainable, falling from £51m to near-zero by 2028.
findings.detail: Bolton holds £51.1m of corporate budget reserves (end 2024/25) which it plans to use to smooth cuts over four years. External auditors Forvis Mazars LLP flagged this approach as unsustainable in their 2022/23 Value for Money report. Reserves are forecast to fall to £26.9m (Mar-26), £7.4m (Mar-27), and £0.7m (Mar-28).
findings.matters: A strategy already criticised by auditors as unsustainable is proceeding, leaving no buffer when the DSG liability becomes unfunded in 2028/29 or if in-year deficits worsen.
findings.quote: this approach to the use of reserves has been challenged by the Council's external auditors (Forvis Mazars LLP) as unsustainable in their 2022/23 Value for Money (VFM) report

findings.paper_title: Budget Report 2026-27 Appendix K - MTFP 26-27 to 29-30
findings.headline: The DSG deficit has grown to £28m and will require coverage from reserves from 2028/29 when the statutory override ends.
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has risen from £20m to £28m. The statutory override allowing councils to defer covering such deficits expires in March 2028, after which Bolton must cover the full amount from reserves. The council acknowledges significant risk it will be unable to do this given the ongoing increases in the deficit.
findings.matters: This unfunded liability will crystallise at exactly the point when the council's reserves are nearly depleted (forecast £0.7m in March 2028), forcing either asset sales, additional borrowing, or service reductions.
findings.figures: £28m (up from £20m); Statutory Override ends March 2028; forecast reserves March 2028 £0.7m
findings.quote: The Statutory Override for the DSG deficit comes to an end in March 2028. From 2026/27 the Council will need to cover this deficit from reserves. Given the ongoing increases in the deficit position there is a significant risk that the Council will be unable to do this.

findings.paper_title: Treasury management and investment strategies for 2026-2027 to 2029-2030
findings.headline: HRA PWLB discount rate expires 31 March 2026 without confirmed extension
findings.detail: The reduced Public Works Loan Board rate for Housing Revenue Account borrowing (60 basis points below standard rate) has been in place since June 2023 and expires 31 March 2026. The paper states the council is hoping for extension 'to be announced in January' but provides no confirmation. If the discount lapses, any new HRA borrowing from April 2026 onwards will cost 60bps more per annum.
findings.matters: A lender would recognize this as a fixed-date cost escalation affecting HRA debt servicing. If Bolton has capital spending plans requiring HRA borrowing after March 2026, the actual cost will be materially higher than currently budgeted, creating an unexpected pressure on HRA finances.
findings.figures: 60 basis points discount (standard rate minus 60bps) expires 31 March 2026; current 1-year PWLB rate 4.81%
findings.quote: Please note, the lower Housing Revenue Account (HRA) PWLB rate started on 15 June 2023 for those authorities with an HRA (standard rate minus 60 bps) and is set to prevail until at least the end of March 2026. Hopefully, there will be a further extension to this discounted rate announced in January.
